pr.body:
**What is this feature?**

Writes to annotations are sometimes rejected on MySQL due to a recurring deadlock with the annotation cleanup job.
Details here: https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/64979

**Why do we need this feature?**

The deadlock seems to be a result of the subquery, under normal circumstances a plain insert and delete should not lock, and there are no extended transactions at play.

This PR splits the subquery into a separate SQL statement. These statements do not share a transaction, and therefore allow locks to flush in between.

Unfortunately we could not reduce this to a single DELETE statement, due to the batching - DELETE LIMIT is not supported on all databases without needing to reintroduce the subquery. The IDs loaded into memory are of bounded size due to the batch size configuration.

**Which issue(s) does this PR fix?**:

https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/64979

**Special notes for your reviewer:**

Please check that:
- [x] It works as expected from a user's perspective.
- [x] If this is a pre-GA feature, it is behind a feature toggle.
- [x] The docs are updated, and if this is a [notable improvement](https://grafana.com/docs/writers-toolkit/writing-guide/contribute-release-notes/#how-to-determine-if-content-belongs-in-a-whats-new-document), it's added to our [What's New](https://grafana.com/docs/writers-toolkit/writing-guide/contribute-release-notes/) doc.
pr.title: Annotations: Split cleanup into separate queries and deletes to avoid deadlocks on MySQL

raw_findings.body: Each iteration re-copies the entire accumulated string via fmt.Sprintf, giving O(n²) allocation and copy cost (e.g., ~32k IDs implies gigabytes of cumulative copying per batch), needlessly slowing the cleanup job and pressuring the GC.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Cleanup batches on SQLite with large batch sizes consume excessive CPU and memory proportional to the square of the batch size.
raw_findings.impact: Each iteration re-copies the entire accumulated string via fmt.Sprintf, giving O(n²) allocation and copy cost (e.g., ~32k IDs implies gigabytes of cumulative copying per batch), needlessly slowing the cleanup job and pressuring the GC.
raw_findings.root_cause: The inline-ID fallback path concatenates the values string with Sprintf inside a loop rather than using an efficient builder.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Build the ID list with a strings.Builder and strconv.FormatInt (or strings.Join over a pre-built slice) instead of repeated Sprintf concatenation.
raw_findings.title: Quadratic string building when inlining IDs into SQLite DELETE statement
raw_findings.trigger: SQLite deployment with AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize configured above 999 (the exact case this branch exists for), producing batches of up to tens of thousands of IDs per cleanup iteration.

raw_findings.failure_mode: A single subtest setup failure cascades into unrelated failures in later subtests sharing the database, degrading test diagnosability.
raw_findings.impact: Leftover annotation and annotation_tag rows from the failed subtest remain in the shared DB, causing subsequent subtests to fail on duplicate primary key inserts (ID: int64(i+1)) or wrong counts, masking the original failure with confusing cascading errors.

raw_findings.suggested_fix: Register the t.Cleanup deletion of annotation and annotation_tag rows before calling createTestAnnotations, so cleanup always runs regardless of setup assertion failures.

finding.verifier_reason: The claim that t.Cleanup registration after createTestAnnotations causes test pollution is incorrect. Go's t.Cleanup registers cleanup functions that run after the test completes regardless of where in the test they are registered. If require/assert fails, the subtest still completes and cleanup runs. The ordering within the test function does not affect cleanup execution.
